title: do something for someone with no receipt
hook: do something for someone with no receipt

segments.voice: Yesterday: kindness, starting with the one in the mirror. Today, kindness with no name on it.

A good deed can come with a little receipt attached. I drove them to the airport. I remembered her birthday. I did the dishes, again. The receipts tend to print themselves. And sometimes the receipt wants to be seen: a thank-you, a mention, a like. Today is about the other kind of giving: no thanks, no credit, maybe nobody even knowing it was you. Four traditions have a lot to say about it.
screen: `THE RECEIPT PRINTS ITSELF.` → `A THANK-YOU, A MENTION, A LIKE.` → `NO RECEIPT.`

segments.voice: Jesus talks about giving to the poor, and says to do it so quietly that, in the King James wording, you "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Your own other hand shouldn't find out. The Jewish scholar Maimonides set out eight levels of giving, from grudging to generous. Near the very top: the giver and the receiver don't know each other's names. And at the top itself: helping someone so they won't need help again, with a gift, a loan, a partnership, a job. In Sikh tradition the word is seva, selfless service, and you can see it in the gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship. Gurdwaras keep a langar, a free kitchen where anyone, of any faith or none, sits and eats together. Volunteers cook, serve and wash up. At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the kitchen feeds a vast number of people every day, served by volunteers whose names the people eating will never learn. And Hindu teaching has a famous line about acting without clinging to the fruits of the action: do the work well, and let go of what it earns you. The reasons differ. For Jesus, the Father sees what's done in secret. For Maimonides, the poor person's dignity matters. In the Hindu line, the doer lets go of the reward. They don't mean the same thing by it. But each of them treats the receipt as the part to throw away.
screen: `LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.` · `MAIMONIDES' LADDER OF GIVING.` · `SEVA AND THE FREE KITCHEN.` · `LET GO OF THE FRUITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For about seventy-five seconds, think of one small thing you could do for someone where nobody would know it was you. Putting a shopping cart back. Refilling the coffee. Paying for something quietly. Pick one. Picture yourself doing it and walking away, no thank-you. Notice what that feels like.
Service. Doing good for someone else, without keeping the receipt. Seventeenth word.
Your line: no receipt. A good deed is already finished the moment it's done. Day seventeen.

screen: `DAY 17 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOU'RE NOT THE ONLY ONE.`

howItsDone: Sikhs volunteer in the langar, the free kitchen of the gurdwara; Jewish and Christian teaching both honor giving that the receiver, or the giver's own circle, never hears about; and Hindu teaching speaks of acting without attachment to reward.

original.note: Gurmukhi, from Sikh tradition: selfless service, done without seeking reward. The word is also Sanskrit (सेवा).

trapdoor: what you thought: being useful, or volunteering now and then.
what it means: doing good for someone without keeping the receipt: no thanks, no credit.
what a scholar hears: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14, ranks eight levels of tzedakah; the top is making the poor person self-sufficient.

notes: Maimonides' eight levels: top is strengthening the poor person's hand by gift, loan, partnership or work so they need no charity; second is giver and receiver unknown to each other. Confirm 'near the very top'.
Golden Temple langar numbers are often reported as 50,000–100,000 a day; the script says only 'a vast number'.
Bhagavad Gita 2.47 paraphrased (action without attachment to its fruits). A Hindu Keeper may refine.
